text.p: Spanish government bond prices ended higher on Monday, after dipping earlier while playing catch-up to other markets after a public holiday last Friday.

Traders said bonos were lifted later in the session by the positive tone in foreign markets, particularly in U.S. Treasuries and Bunds, with domestic factors counting for little in the traditionally sluggish August holiday trade.

"The market is very apathetic and only responds to very concrete forces," one analyst said. "Foreign markets are leading and fundamentally we are awaiting the FOMC meeting tomorrow and the setting of the repo by the Bundesbank."

Most economists do not see the U.S. Federal Reserve changing its interest rates because they see no inflationary pressures. Fears that the Bundesbank might signal a monetary tightening by setting a variable rate evaporated as the dollar weakened against the mark.

But some warned that should the German central bank move to raise rates in the short term in defiance of expectations rather than later in the year, it would put considerable pressure on Spanish long bond yields.
The Bank of Spain was seen almost globally as holding its key money rate at 5.25 percent until Congress debates the 1998 draft budget in September.
